test_title: PYST 30: SSC CHSL - Quantitative Aptitude (Held On: 20 March, 2023 Shift 2)
subject: maths
question: A train of length 300 metres crosses a tree in 20 seconds and crosses another train of the same length travelling in opposite direction in 25 seconds. What is the speed of the second train?
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Speed of the first train = Distance ÷ Time = 300 ÷ 20 = 15 m/s

Relative speed of both trains (opposite direction) = Total Distance ÷ Time = (300 + 300) ÷ 25 = 600 ÷ 25 = 24 m/s

Speed of the second train = Relative Speed − Speed of first train = 24 − 15 = 9 m/s

**∴ The correct answer is 9 m/s.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/7fe2cb9f8b0b10992f5f16c8700501c9f9a876b4fdc5916368e2d0baba0e4e17.png] 

**Given:**

Length of Train 1 (L₁) = 300 m

Time to cross a tree = 20 s

Length of Train 2 (L₂) = 300 m

Time to cross each other = 25 s

**Formula Used:**

Speed = Distance ÷ Time

Relative speed in opposite direction = S₁ + S₂

**Calculations:**

⇒ Speed of Train 1 (S₁) = 300 ÷ 20 = 15 m/s

⇒ Total distance to cross each other = L₁ + L₂ = 300 + 300 = 600 m

⇒ Relative speed = Total Distance ÷ Crossing Time

⇒ S₁ + S₂ = 600 ÷ 25

⇒ 15 + S₂ = 24

⇒ S₂ = 24 − 15

⇒ S₂ = 9 m/s

**∴ The correct answer is 9 m/s.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Relative Speed in Same Direction

When two trains travel in the same direction, their relative speed is the difference of their individual speeds: S = S₁ − S₂ (where S₁ > S₂).

Relative Speed in Opposite Direction

When two trains travel towards each other, their relative speed is the sum of their individual speeds: S = S₁ + S₂.

Crossing a Stationary Object

If a train crosses a pole, standing man, or tree, the distance covered is equal to the length of the train alone: D = L₁.

Crossing a Platform/Bridge

If a train crosses a platform or another train, the total distance covered is the sum of their lengths: D = L₁ + L₂.
